newsitem.title: USA: U.S. worker compensation up 0.6 percent in quarter.
newsitem.headline: U.S. worker compensation up 0.6 percent in quarter.

text.p: U.S. workers' compensation gains slowed in the first three months of 1997 as nearly flat benefit costs moderated the effect of a sharp jump in wages and salaries, the Labor Department said on Tuesday.
Pay and benefits combined rose 0.6 percent in the first quarter of the year after a 0.8 percent gain in the fourth quarter of 1996, the department said in its quarterly Employment Cost Index report.
Wall Street economists surveyed by Reuters had predicted a much sharper 0.9 percent rise in workers' compensation for the first quarter.

Wages and salaries, which represent about 70 percent of the index, jumped 0.9 percent in the first quarter, the largest gain in a year, after a 0.8 percent rise in the fourth quarter, the department said.
Benefit costs rose a scant 0.1 percent, matching their smallest increase in a year, after a 0.7 percent gain in the fourth quarter, it said.

Financial markets had been anticipating the release of the index for further clues of whether growing tightness in labour markets is raising salaries and benefit levels to the point where they could become an inflationary threat.

Federal Reserve policymakers, who raised short-term interest rates a quarter of a percentage point last month to help defuse such a threat and are expected by many economists to do so again, are thought to be keeping close tabs on labour costs.
Another economic indicator closely followed by the Fed and financial markets is the department's monthly unemployment report, which will be released on Friday.
In the 12 months ended March 31, total compensation rose 2.9 percent, compared with 2.9 percent in all of 1996 and 2.8 percent in the 12 months ended March 31, 1996.
Wages and salaries in the 12 months ended March 31 rose 3.3 percent, identical to the five-year-high increase of 1996, after a 3.1 percent gain in the 12 months ended March 31, 1996.

Employers' cost of providing benefits, including medical insurance, rose 2 percent in the 12 months ended March 31, the same as for 1996, after a 1.8 percent gain in the 12 months ended March 31, 1996.

Before the first quarter, benefit cost increases had begun to rebound after slowing in late 1995 and holding steady in early 1996 as employers shifted a greater share of health care costs onto their employees and opted for cheaper managed care plans.

Many economists expect benefit costs to continue accelerating, arguing that employers' health care costs savings were a one-time occurance and that medical care costs are set to increase more rapidly.

Compensation for private industry workers in the first quarter rose 0.6 percent after climbing 0.7 percent in the fourth quarter, while state and local government workers' compensation rose 0.5 percent after a 0.8 percent rise in the fourth quarter.
